result:
The rain does not ask permission. It simply arrives, tapping a loose, patient rhythm against the café windowpane. The glass fogs in soft, wandering shapes, and the street beyond becomes a watercolor of amber and grey—the streetlamps bleeding downward, the red of a bicycle helmet smearing into wet pavement like a thumbprint in mud.

I watch a woman in a yellow coat hurry across. Her movement is sudden, almost violent against the slow smear of everything else. Then she is gone, and the street resumes its long exhalation. A pigeon lands on the bus stop bench, tilts its head with the profound suspicion of an employee clocking in, and takes off.

There is something I have always loved about the hour before dark, especially when it rains. The world stops being sharp. All the edges that made you feel small and precise and responsible soften. Your name is a suggestion rather than a fact. The coffee goes cold and that is fine. You do not have to be useful. You can simply be a warm animal in a glass room, listening to the sky drip, feeling the strange small mercy of doing nothing for five more minutes.

The rain will stop. The fog will dry. You will stand up, the coffee will be embarrassing, and the street will be sharp, and the day will demand its ordinary weight. But not yet, not this minute. The window is a soft grey cathedral, and you are allowed to sit in it.
